newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain government releases secret "dirty war" files.
newsitem.headline: Spain government releases secret "dirty war" files.

text.p: Spain's government, under orders from the Supreme Court, released secret files on Friday that could prove former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez orchestrated a 1980s "dirty war" against Basque separatist guerrillas.
The court last month overturned an earlier decision by the present conservative government to keep the documents, from Spain's military intelligence agency CESID, classified.

"With this (decision), we hope not only to comply with the Supreme Court request but also to contribute as much as possible to clarifying the truth," Defence Minister Eduardo Serra told a news conference.

Former associates say Gonzalez ran the campaign of killings, kidnappings and torture to combat the violent Basque separatist movement ETA. Lawyers prosecuting "dirty war" cases say the so-called CESID papers could prove he was involved.
From 1983-1987, shadowy agents of "anti-terrorist" death squads killed 28 people. No fewer than one third of the victims were targetted by mistake.
ETA, which stands for Basque Homeland and Freedom, has killed some 800 people in a 29-year fight for an independent state encompassing parts of northern Spain and southern France.
Lower courts investigating the "dirty war" asked the Supreme Court for the documents which they say contain vital information needed to prosecute former senior officials and security chiefs.

The Supreme Court ordered the government to open 13 of 16 documents requested which can now be introduced as evidence. The court said it kept three documents secret because they would compromise CESID operations or violate international agreements on exchanging intelligence.
The documents first came to light in a complicated intrigue which ex-officials on trial for the "dirty war" have said was a conspiracy of aggrieved rivals, judges and journalists.
Spanish newspapers have already published copies of the documents allegedly stolen by a former spy for the military intelligence agency. But their authenticity was questionable.
In the early 1980s, ETA was killing about one person a week and the government was under pressure to respond.
The documents lay out the structure and objectives of the death squads and show many levels of the security services were involved. They indicate top officials were in the know.
The CESID files recommended finding methods not subject to legal restraint to fight ETA and sanctioned kidnapping and armed action to combat guerrillas based in southern France.
The files also had suggestions on how to cover-up the war.
"It is essential these actions appear to be settling of accounts or internal reprisals so that media coverage always leaves doubt about the real author of the deeds," one said.
Gonzalez's former interior minister Jose Barrionuevo and senior security officials have already been charged in "dirty war" cases and could go on trial this year.
Gonzalez has maintained his innocence and the Supreme Court has decided against questioning him so far.

Even though the ruling Popular Party used the "dirty war" scandal in its campaign to unseat Gonzalez in last year's election, it decided in August to keep the documents under wraps. Gonzalez lost the election after 13 years in power.
The government said then that the publication would deter other countries from sharing intelligence with Spain.
